title: sudo, find, grep and safe practice
summary: Using privilege and search tools without causing incidents — including the exact commands to investigate rather than guess.

sections.heading: sudo is not 'be root'
sections.html:
sudo runs a command as another user according to /etc/sudoers (edited with visudo, never directly). Points that matter operationally:

  • Least privilege is expressible: grant a specific command, not ALL.
  • sudo does not fix ownership problems. Running an editor as root on a config file can leave it root-owned and unreadable by the service — a self-inflicted version of the bug you were fixing.
  • Redirection happens in your shell, before sudo runs: sudo echo x > /etc/file fails with permission denied because the shell opened the file, not sudo. Use sudo tee or sudo sh -c '...'.
  • sudo caching means a second command may not prompt; scripts should not rely on interaction.
# safely append a line to a root-owned fileecho 'Setting=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/app/app.conf
# sudo the whole pipeline when neededsudo sh -c 'grep -c error /var/log/app.log > /tmp/count'

sections.heading: find: the investigation tool
sections.html:
# biggest files under /var, one filesystemsudo find /var -xdev -type f -size +200M -printf '%s\t%p\n' | sort -rn | head
# recently modified config (change analysis)sudo find /etc -type f -mmin -60 -ls
# files that are world-writable (a real security check)sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -print 2>/dev/null
# setuid binaries outside package-managed pathssudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
# delete files older than 30 days in a scratch directory onlyfind /home/me/netquest-practice -type f -mtime +30 -delete

Two safety habits: always bound find to a specific path and use -xdev to avoid traversing into network or virtual filesystems, and never combine -delete with an unbounded path. Preview the matches by running the same command without -delete first.

sections.heading: grep and locate
sections.html:
# which config file sets this directive?sudo grep -rn --include='*.conf' 'Listen' /etc
# case-insensitive, with line numbers, skipping binariesgrep -rniI 'max_clients' /etc/app
# fixed string (no regex metachars) with contextgrep -nF -A2 -B2 'Connection refused' /var/log/messages
# files by name, database-backed (fast, possibly stale)locate -i 'app.conf' | head
# rebuild the database if locate is emptysudo updatedb

Keep in mind the division of labour: find searches by metadata (name, size, time, permissions), grep searches content, locate is a fast but stale index. In an incident, find with -mmin is often the fastest way to discover what changed.

sections.heading: Safe practice rules for this application's exercises
sections.html:
Every exercise in NetQuest uses a directory you create, never system paths:

mkdir -p ~/netquest-practice && cd ~/netquest-practice
  • Never run chmod -R or chown -R on /, /etc, /usr or /var.
  • Never delete anything you did not create.
  • Practice with chmod on files in the practice directory and read the effect with ls -l.
  • Do not change firewall rules, routing or DNS configuration to 'test' something against the live system; simulate in the lab instead, or use a container.

checks.prompt: Why does `sudo echo test > /etc/app.conf` fail with 'Permission denied'?
options: The shell performs the redirection as your user before sudo runs
checks.explanation: Redirection is set up by the calling shell, which lacks write permission. Use `echo test | sudo tee /etc/app.conf`.

why_wrong.0: A password prompt is not a permission error.

checks.prompt: Which command best shows what changed in /etc during the last hour?
checks.explanation: -mmin -60 filters by modification time within the last 60 minutes — ideal change analysis after an incident.

why_wrong.1: That searches for the literal word 'changed'.
why_wrong.2: locate searches names in a stale index.

connect.title: Incidents
connect.text: 'What changed?' is answered by find -mmin, package logs and audit trails, not by intuition.

connect.title: Safety
connect.text: These habits are why NetQuest never asks you to modify system configuration as an exercise.

connect.title: Case study 10
connect.text: Uses exactly these commands on files inside the practice directory.

interview.q: How would you find the config file responsible for a setting?
interview.a: grep -rn --include over /etc to find the directive, then check the service unit for EnvironmentFile or command-line overrides, since the last value wins. Distro defaults under /usr/lib are read-only references.

interview.q: Why is chmod 777 a bad fix?
interview.a: It grants write access to everyone, which is an integrity and security problem, and it hides the real cause (wrong owner, missing group membership or missing traversal bit). It also makes future permission problems impossible to diagnose.
